definition: Challenges related to determining whether information, influence, cognitive security, or related activities are effective, attributable, comparable, and worth prioritizing.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude items primarily about data access/observability problems, forecasting uncertainty, or strategic narrative failures unless the main issue is measuring effects.
inclusionCriteria: Use for items about MOE/MOP ambiguity, causal attribution, baselines, ROI, effect size, audience reception, prioritization metrics, evaluation design, or assessment credibility.
name: Measurement, Attribution & Assessment Gaps
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Forecasting, Complexity & Uncertainty, which concerns anticipating future conditions; distinct from Data, Privacy, Surveillance & Observability Problems, which concerns whether relevant data can be collected or seen; distinct from Strategic Communication failures, which concerns poor message/narrative design.

definition: Risks and constraints arising from legal authorities, constitutional protections, permissions, rules of engagement, jurisdictional boundaries, consent requirements, and civil-liberties concerns.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude broad policy lag or regulation issues unless tied to specific legal authority or rights constraints; exclude legitimacy/trust issues unless the legal/civil-liberties tension is central.
inclusionCriteria: Use for First Amendment concerns, domestic/foreign audience blur, delegation of authorities, ROE, consent law, intelligence authorities, legal review, or fears of propaganda against domestic publics.
name: Authorities, Legal Constraints & Civil-Liberties Tensions
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Governance, Policy & Regulatory Lag, which is about policy or regulatory frameworks not keeping pace; distinct from Trust, Legitimacy & Institutional Credibility Erosion, which concerns perceived credibility and legitimacy outcomes; distinct from Institutional Fragmentation, which concerns organizational coordination.

definition: Constraints resulting from insufficient resources, funding, staffing, prioritization, or sustained investment relative to the scale or importance of cognitive/information challenges.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude workforce skill gaps, acquisition friction, or institutional coordination problems unless the main barrier is resources or prioritization.
inclusionCriteria: Use for underinvestment, budget disparities, unfunded mandates, mismatch between stated concern and actual funding, lack of dedicated resources, or low organizational priority.
name: Resource, Funding & Prioritization Gaps
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Workforce, Expertise & Training Gaps, which concerns human capital and skills; distinct from Technology Adoption, Transition & Acquisition Friction, which concerns transition/acquisition pathways; distinct from Institutional Fragmentation, which concerns coordination rather than resource level.

definition: Barriers in moving technologies, tools, prototypes, or analytic systems from development into operational use because of acquisition, transition, workflow, usability, or integration problems.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude risks caused by AI/model reliability, cyber exposure, or data overload unless the main issue is adoption/transition/acquisition.
inclusionCriteria: Use for acquisition lag, tool adoption failure, lab-to-ops transition, missing workflow design, over-engineered systems, poor user fit, or failure to integrate tools into operational processes.
name: Technology Adoption, Transition & Acquisition Friction
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from AI, Automation & Model Reliability Risks, which concerns behavior and reliability of automated systems; distinct from OPSEC/Cyber/Infrastructure risks, which concerns technical exposure; distinct from Resource gaps, which concerns funding rather than transition mechanics.

definition: Challenges created by synthetic or manipulated media, declining ability to verify authenticity, blurred distinctions between true and false content, and erosion of shared evidentiary standards.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude general AI reliability problems, platform incentive problems, or trust erosion unless the main mechanism is authenticity/verification collapse.
inclusionCriteria: Use for deepfakes, authenticity crisis, verification failures, fact-checking blind spots, truth/falsehood ambiguity, deceptive omissions, manipulated evidence, or provenance uncertainty.
name: Synthetic Media, Verification & Authenticity Collapse
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from AI risks, which focus on model behavior; distinct from Platform/Algorithmic distortions, which focus on distribution and attention incentives; distinct from Trust/Legitimacy erosion, which focuses on institutional credibility outcomes.

definition: Challenges related to collecting, accessing, interpreting, governing, or protecting data needed for influence, cognitive security, or assessment in environments shaped by privacy concerns and surveillance capabilities.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude assessment problems unless the main challenge is measurement logic rather than data observability; exclude legal/civil-liberties tensions unless the legal authority issue is primary.
inclusionCriteria: Use for digital dust, VR/BCI biometrics, RF collection, private channels, OSINT/PAI/CAI ambiguity, petabyte-scale data overload, observability limits, or privacy-sensitive monitoring.
name: Data, Privacy, Surveillance & Observability Problems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Measurement gaps, which concern evaluating effect and causality; distinct from Authorities/Legal constraints, which concern legal permissions and rights; distinct from OPSEC/Cyber risks, which concern technical exposure and vulnerabilities.

definition: Challenges created by fragmented publics, microcommunities, platform migration, highly segmented audiences, personalized exploitation, and difficulty understanding or reaching target audience subgroups.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude platform algorithm problems unless distribution mechanics are primary; exclude strategic narrative failure unless the core issue is audience segmentation rather than message design.
inclusionCriteria: Use for microcommunities, platform migration, Gen Z knowledge gaps, personalized exploitation, diaspora segmentation, audience segmentation, heterogeneous audience reception, or targeting complexity.
name: Audience Fragmentation & Micro-Targeting Complexity
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Platform/Algorithmic Distortions, which concerns platform incentives and algorithms; distinct from Strategic Communication failures, which concerns narrative design; distinct from Societal Polarization, which concerns broader identity and democratic resilience risks.

definition: Risks rooted in individual or group cognition, cognitive biases, heuristics, fatigue, emotional states, behavioral vulnerabilities, and limits of attention, reasoning, or self-regulation.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude societal-level polarization, audience segmentation, or platform algorithmic dynamics unless the central mechanism is cognitive/behavioral vulnerability.
inclusionCriteria: Use for heuristics, fatigue, cognitive load, de-individuation, myth/history confusion, emotional exhaustion, overtrust, persuasion vulnerability, or cognitive limitations.
name: Human Cognition, Bias & Behavioral Vulnerability
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Societal Polarization, which concerns social identity and democratic resilience; distinct from Audience Fragmentation, which concerns segmentation; distinct from Platform distortions, which concerns algorithmic and attention-economy mechanisms.

definition: Failures in framing, narrative design, symbolic communication, public diplomacy, or meaning-making that prevent actors from shaping perceptions, interpreting events, or occupying important narrative opportunities.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude audience segmentation problems, trust erosion, or measurement issues unless the central problem is narrative/message design or meaning-making.
inclusionCriteria: Use for misframing Taiwan, weak narrative design, myths/symbols, public diplomacy confusion, failure to occupy narrative windows, poor strategic messaging, or narrative incoherence.
name: Strategic Communication, Narrative & Meaning-Making Failures
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Audience Fragmentation, which concerns who is being addressed; distinct from Trust/Legitimacy, which concerns credibility of institutions; distinct from Measurement gaps, which concerns assessing effects.

definition: Challenges caused by nonlinear systems, unpredictable shocks, foresight limitations, wrong mental models, timing uncertainty, entropy, and difficulty anticipating complex information-environment dynamics.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude measurement/assessment gaps unless evaluating past effects is central; exclude strategic narrative failures unless the issue is future uncertainty rather than narrative design.
inclusionCriteria: Use for nonlinearity, foresight gaps, unpredictable shocks, entropy, wrong mental models, crisis timing, uncertainty about second-order effects, or complex adaptive behavior.
name: Forecasting, Complexity & Uncertainty
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Measurement/Attribution gaps, which concern assessing observed effects; distinct from Strategic Communication failures, which concerns framing and meaning-making; distinct from AI/Automation risks unless uncertainty is specifically caused by model behavior.

definition: Barriers caused by fragmented institutions, siloed responsibilities, misaligned incentives, unclear ownership, or weak coordination across agencies, sectors, commands, or organizations.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude items mainly about doctrine gaps, legal authorities, resource scarcity, or workforce skill shortages unless fragmentation/coordination is the central problem.
inclusionCriteria: Use for interagency silos, public-private mismatch, GCC duplication, cross-sector communication gaps, unclear lead agency, poor handoffs, or coordination breakdowns.
name: Institutional Fragmentation & Coordination Barriers
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Doctrine, Force Design & Organizational Design Gaps, which concerns formal concepts, roles, force structure, and organizational design; distinct from Governance, Policy & Regulatory Lag, which concerns rules and policy frameworks; distinct from Resource gaps, which concerns funding and prioritization.

definition: Challenges caused by governance systems, policies, treaties, regulations, curricula, or oversight mechanisms failing to keep pace with technological, informational, or operational change.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude specific legal authority questions, operational coordination failures, or technology adoption friction unless the core issue is policy/regulatory lag.
inclusionCriteria: Use for outdated treaties, privacy law gaps, platform regulation gaps, curriculum fragmentation, policy lag behind technology, governance mismatch, or inadequate oversight architecture.
name: Governance, Policy & Regulatory Lag
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Authorities, Legal Constraints & Civil-Liberties Tensions, which concerns permissions and rights; distinct from Technology Adoption, Transition & Acquisition Friction, which concerns getting tools into practice; distinct from Institutional Fragmentation, which concerns coordination among entities.

definition: Problems stemming from unsettled doctrine, unclear concepts, inadequate force design, weak organizational structures, or treating information-related capabilities as peripheral rather than integral.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude coordination failures between existing organizations, legal authorities, or workforce training problems unless the central issue is formal design/doctrine.
inclusionCriteria: Use for unsettled IE definitions, weak control measures, force design gaps, IO treated as irregular/afterthought, unclear organizational roles, or inadequate integration into planning constructs.
name: Doctrine, Force Design & Organizational Design Gaps
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Institutional Fragmentation, which concerns coordination among entities; distinct from Workforce gaps, which concerns skills and expertise; distinct from Governance/Policy lag, which concerns policies and regulation rather than operational doctrine or force design.

definition: Risks arising from artificial intelligence, automation, machine learning, or model-driven systems that may be unreliable, biased, opaque, misused, adversarially manipulated, or overtrusted.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude general synthetic media authenticity problems unless the main issue is AI/model reliability; exclude technology adoption friction unless the problem is transition rather than model behavior.
inclusionCriteria: Use for LLM misuse, hallucination, AI bias, model drift, black-box AI, adversarial ML, automation overtrust, unreliable recommendations, or automated decision-support errors.
name: AI, Automation & Model Reliability Risks
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Synthetic Media, Verification & Authenticity Collapse, which focuses on content authenticity and deepfakes; distinct from Platform/Algorithmic Distortions, which focuses on attention systems and recommendation environments; distinct from Technology Adoption friction, which concerns implementation pathways.

definition: Risks arising from platform design, recommender systems, algorithmic opacity, attention-market incentives, content moderation dynamics, and incentive structures that distort information exposure.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude synthetic media verification, AI model reliability, or audience fragmentation unless the main mechanism is platform/algorithmic distribution or attention incentives.
inclusionCriteria: Use for recommendation manipulation, clickbait incentives, moderation backfire, attention atomization, algorithmic opacity, engagement-maximizing systems, or platform-amplified polarization.
name: Platform, Algorithmic & Attention-Economy Distortions
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Synthetic Media risks, which concern authenticity of content; distinct from Audience Fragmentation, which concerns segmentation and microcommunities; distinct from Societal Polarization, which concerns broader social division outcomes.

definition: Risks caused by vulnerable devices, networks, infrastructure, cyber dependencies, technical signatures, spoofing, and connective technological exposure that can be exploited by adversaries.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude data privacy/observability problems unless the main issue is technical exposure; exclude technology adoption friction unless the issue is implementation rather than vulnerability.
inclusionCriteria: Use for personal devices, GNSS/PNT spoofing, medical IoT, solar/space vulnerabilities, connective tissue attacks, cyber exposure, infrastructure dependencies, or operational security failures.
name: OPSEC, Cyber, Infrastructure & Technical Exposure Risks
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Data/Privacy/Observability, which concerns data access and surveillance; distinct from Technology Adoption friction, which concerns moving tools into use; distinct from AI reliability, which concerns model behavior.

definition: Risks involving declining trust in institutions, media, government, or information sources; loss of legitimacy; perceived abandonment; and heightened public sensitivity to propaganda or manipulation.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude legal/civil-liberties tensions unless rights/authorities are central; exclude societal polarization unless broader social division rather than institutional credibility is central.
inclusionCriteria: Use for declining trust, institutional legitimacy loss, media credibility decline, perceived abandonment, public sensitivity to propaganda, credibility deficits, or distrust of official messaging.
name: Trust, Legitimacy & Institutional Credibility Erosion
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Societal Polarization, which concerns identity-based or democratic resilience risks; distinct from Authorities/Legal Constraints, which concerns formal permissions and rights; distinct from Synthetic Media risks, which concerns authenticity mechanisms.

definition: Societal-level risks involving polarization, identity conflict, democratic vulnerability, radicalization, social capital decline, and erosion of shared meaning or collective resilience.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude individual cognitive vulnerabilities, institutional trust erosion, or audience segmentation unless the main issue is society-level identity/polarization/resilience.
inclusionCriteria: Use for domestic radicalization, societal divisions, crisis of meaning, democratic vulnerability, social capital decline, identity conflict, or resilience of democratic publics.
name: Societal Polarization, Identity & Democratic Resilience Risks
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Human Cognition/Bias, which concerns individual cognitive mechanisms; distinct from Trust/Legitimacy, which concerns institutional credibility; distinct from Audience Fragmentation, which concerns segmentation and targeting complexity.

definition: Risks arising when adversaries possess structural, normative, cost, doctrinal, or operational advantages in information, influence, lawfare, transparency, or strategic competition.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude resource gaps or platform distortions unless the main issue is adversary comparative advantage; exclude legal/civil-liberties constraints unless framed as an adversary asymmetry.
inclusionCriteria: Use for PRC/Russia advantages, adversary cost advantage, transparent battlefield exploitation, lawfare/normative asymmetry, authoritarian information advantages, or asymmetric burden on democratic actors.
name: Strategic Asymmetry & Adversary Advantage
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Resource/Funding gaps, which are internal capacity constraints; distinct from Authorities/Legal constraints, which concern legal permissions; distinct from Strategic Communication failures, which concern narrative design rather than comparative adversary advantage.

definition: Human capital challenges involving inadequate expertise, weak career fields, training shortfalls, missing taxonomies, limited literacy, language bias, or insufficient practitioner capacity.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude resource/funding gaps, doctrine/force design gaps, or technology adoption problems unless the central issue is human skill/expertise.
inclusionCriteria: Use for career field weakness, narrative design skill gaps, media literacy gaps, cognitive security taxonomy gaps, English-only bias, training gaps, expertise shortages, or insufficient professional development.
name: Workforce, Expertise & Training Gaps
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinct from Resource/Funding gaps, which concerns money and prioritization; distinct from Doctrine/Force Design gaps, which concerns formal structures; distinct from Technology Adoption friction, which concerns tools and transition pathways.

definition: Use for future-oriented claims that information, cognition, narrative, perception, and influence will become more central to warfare, deterrence, strategic competition, and national security outcomes.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude specific AI/deepfake predictions unless the main claim is about the broader centrality of information warfare. Exclude generic media trends unless linked to strategic influence or conflict.
inclusionCriteria: Predictions about IO/OIE becoming a core warfighting function; cognition as a future battlespace; perception management as decisive; narrative competition as central to strategy; increasing importance of cognitive security.
name: Cognitive / Information Warfare Centrality
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from AI-Enabled Influence when the emphasis is not the enabling technology but the strategic elevation of cognition/information. Different from Media Ecosystems when the focus is military/strategic centrality rather than attention dynamics.

definition: Use for predictions that AI, generative media, autonomous content systems, or synthetic artifacts will transform influence, deception, persuasion, targeting, or information operations.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude broad AI-enabled decision support or C2 integration unless the prediction is about influence or synthetic media. Exclude non-AI platform amplification trends.
inclusionCriteria: Deepfakes; synthetic audio/video; AI-generated propaganda; scalable personalized persuasion; AI-assisted microtargeting; automated influence campaigns; synthetic personas or content farms.
name: AI-Enabled Influence & Synthetic Media
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Human–AI Teaming when the focus is outward influence content rather than human-machine work processes. Different from Trust/Verification when the emphasis is production of synthetic media rather than the epistemic response.

definition: Use for predictions that AI will become embedded in human reasoning, decision-making, education, planning, command, analysis, or everyday cognition.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude AI-generated influence content unless the main point is how humans work with AI to create or assess it. Exclude general AI governance predictions.
inclusionCriteria: AI copilots; augmented analysts; AI in C2; AI tutors; human-machine teaming; cognitive offloading; AI replacing or reshaping knowledge work; decision aids integrated into operations.
name: Human–AI Teaming & Cognitive Integration
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from AI-Enabled Influence when the focus is internal augmentation of cognition/work. Different from Operational Tempo when the focus is human-AI integration rather than speed advantage.

definition: Use for predictions that personalized feeds, recommendation systems, micro-publics, and individualized media environments will weaken shared reality, common knowledge, or social consensus.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude general media competition unless personalization or fragmentation is central. Exclude trust/authenticity issues unless driven by algorithmic fragmentation.
inclusionCriteria: Filter bubbles; micro-publics; individualized information realities; algorithmic curation; personalization; tailored epistemic environments; audience segmentation leading to divergent beliefs.
name: Algorithmic Personalization & Fragmented Realities
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Media Ecosystems when the focus is fragmentation of shared reality rather than media format or attention competition. Different from Trust/Verification when the issue is differentiated exposure rather than inability to verify authenticity.

definition: Use for predictions about the future difficulty of knowing what is true, verifying authenticity, maintaining institutional trust, or protecting shared epistemic foundations.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude synthetic media production unless the focus is verification/trust consequences. Exclude social cohesion claims unless epistemic trust or legitimacy is central.
inclusionCriteria: Provenance systems; authentication; authenticity collapse; institutional legitimacy crises; trust erosion; verification challenges; content credentials; source reliability problems.
name: Trust, Verification, & Epistemic Security
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from AI-Enabled Influence when the core issue is verifying truth rather than creating synthetic content. Different from Societal Transformation when the concern is epistemic security rather than identity or cohesion broadly.

definition: Use for predictions that competition below armed conflict will become continuous, normalized, and multi-instrument, especially through cyber, information, legal, political, economic, and psychological means.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude conventional warfighting adaptation unless framed as below-threshold competition. Exclude broad geopolitical realignment unless tied to continuous gray-zone methods.
inclusionCriteria: Gray-zone operations; competition below threshold; hybrid warfare; continuous campaigning; persistent engagement; lawfare; cyber-enabled coercion; political warfare.
name: Persistent Competition & Gray-Zone Conflict
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Geopolitical Competition when the emphasis is mode of conflict rather than alignment or great-power structure. Different from Cognitive Warfare Centrality when the focus includes broader below-threshold instruments, not only information/cognition.

definition: Use for predictions that institutions must change structures, doctrine, governance models, workforce roles, authorities, or operating concepts to remain effective in future information and technology environments.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude workforce-specific training/talent unless institutional redesign is central. Exclude regulation or standards unless about broader institutional rule-setting.
inclusionCriteria: Doctrine reform; new offices or commands; organizational redesign; governance adaptation; institutional learning; new operational concepts; bureaucratic transformation.
name: Institutional Adaptation & Organizational Transformation
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Workforce Evolution when the emphasis is organization-level structure rather than people pipelines. Different from Governance/Regulation when the focus is internal adaptation rather than external rules.

definition: Use for predictions that commercial firms, platforms, cloud providers, infrastructure owners, venture ecosystems, and private-sector actors will become central to national security, influence, and information competition.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude general technology trends unless the role of commercial actors is central. Exclude cross-sector regulation unless the main issue is governance rules.
inclusionCriteria: Platform power; corporate control of infrastructure; cloud providers; private AI firms; defense-commercial partnerships; venture capital; public-private integration; commercial data ecosystems.
name: Public–Private Integration & Corporate Power
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Technology Competition when the focus is actor/institutional role of companies rather than the technology itself. Different from Governance/Regulation when the focus is dependence on or integration with corporate power.

definition: Use for predictions about evolving media formats, creator economies, platform logics, virality, attention scarcity, short-form content, agenda setting, and narrative amplification dynamics.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude personalization-specific reality fragmentation unless algorithmic individualized exposure is central. Exclude synthetic media unless AI generation/authenticity is central.
inclusionCriteria: Short-form video; creator ecosystems; virality; engagement competition; platform migration; attention economy; media fragmentation; narrative amplification through media systems.
name: Media Ecosystems & Attention Competition
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Algorithmic Personalization when the focus is media ecology and attention competition rather than individualized realities. Different from Cognitive Warfare Centrality when the emphasis is communication ecosystem dynamics rather than strategic-military centrality.

definition: Use for predictions that future advantage will depend on faster decision cycles, machine-speed adaptation, persistent sensing, continuous access, predictive analytics, and real-time operational awareness.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude AI teaming unless speed, sensing, or decision advantage is the central predicted effect. Exclude emerging tech lists unless tied to operational tempo or sensing.
inclusionCriteria: Decision advantage; machine-speed C2; ubiquitous sensing; persistent ISR; anticipatory analytics; continuous monitoring; rapid adaptation; operational tempo acceleration.
name: Operational Tempo, Persistent Sensing, & Decision Advantage
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Human–AI Teaming when focus is speed and operational advantage rather than human cognitive integration. Different from Cyber/Space/XR/Bio when focus is operational effect rather than technology domain.

definition: Use for predictions that strategic competition will increasingly center on emerging technology domains such as cyber, space, quantum, XR, bioengineering, IoT, blockchain/web3, advanced sensing, and related infrastructures.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude AI influence predictions unless AI is part of a broader emerging-tech competition claim. Exclude operational tempo claims unless the technology domain itself is the focus.
inclusionCriteria: Cyber futures; space systems; quantum; XR/metaverse; bioengineering; IoT; blockchain/web3; advanced sensing; convergence of emerging technologies.
name: Cyber, Space, XR, Bio, & Emerging Technology Competition
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Operational Tempo when the focus is the technology landscape rather than decision speed. Different from Governance/Regulation when the focus is competition in technologies rather than rule-setting around them.

definition: Use for predictions about major-power competition, authoritarian coordination, alliance restructuring, geopolitical realignment, decoupling, standards competition, and governance model contests.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude gray-zone methods unless the focus is continuous below-threshold operations. Exclude specific emerging technologies unless they are used as instruments in broader geopolitical alignment.
inclusionCriteria: China/Russia/Iran alignment; NATO/partner realignment; decoupling; great-power competition; authoritarian governance export; standards diplomacy; geopolitical blocs.
name: Geopolitical Competition & Authoritarian Alignment
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Persistent Competition when the focus is global alignment and strategic order rather than day-to-day conflict methods. Different from Governance/Regulation when the focus is geopolitical contest rather than specific rule-making mechanisms.

definition: Use for predictions about demographic, cultural, identity, civic, social-capital, polarization, and cohesion changes that affect society’s resilience or vulnerability.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude epistemic trust issues unless the emphasis is authenticity/verification. Exclude workforce-specific trends unless tied to broader social transformation.
inclusionCriteria: Identity fragmentation; polarization; social capital decline; demographic change; civic trust; crisis of meaning; social cohesion; cosmopolitanism; community transformation.
name: Societal Transformation, Identity, & Social Cohesion
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Trust/Verification when the focus is social cohesion or identity rather than truth authentication. Different from Non-State Actors when the focus is broad society rather than specific distributed actors.

definition: Use for predictions that future advantage will depend on specialized skills, IO talent, AI fluency, interdisciplinary expertise, new personnel models, education transformation, and adaptive workforce pipelines.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude institution-wide redesign unless talent/workforce is the main focus. Exclude general education impacts from AI unless tied to future national security or influence workforce needs.
inclusionCriteria: IO career fields; AI literacy; interdisciplinary training; talent exchanges; education reform; specialist workforce; new personnel systems; human capital pipelines.
name: Workforce, Talent, & Human Capital Evolution
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Institutional Adaptation when the focus is people, skills, and pipelines rather than structures. Different from Human–AI Teaming when the focus is workforce development rather than use of AI in cognition.

definition: Use for predictions about future legal regimes, governance frameworks, standards-setting, oversight systems, censorship regimes, AI governance, evaluation rules, and institutional control mechanisms.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude internal organizational adaptation unless the focus is public rule-setting or oversight. Exclude geopolitical competition unless the rule-setting contest is central.
inclusionCriteria: AI regulation; platform governance; standards-setting; censorship regimes; legal competition; oversight institutions; compliance frameworks; governance of emerging tech.
name: Governance, Regulation, & Institutional Rule-Setting
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Institutional Adaptation when the focus is external governance and rules rather than organizational change. Different from Geopolitical Competition when the focus is mechanisms of rule-setting rather than strategic alignment.

definition: Use for predictions that future sociotechnical systems will become more interconnected, unstable, hard to forecast, and prone to cascading effects, shocks, or tipping points.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude general future uncertainty unless complexity/nonlinearity is explicit or central. Exclude specific technology predictions unless framed as cascading sociotechnical risk.
inclusionCriteria: Nonlinearity; cascading disruption; volatility; systems complexity; tipping points; uncertainty; interconnected risk; unpredictable shocks; emergent effects.
name: Complexity, Volatility, & Nonlinear Dynamics
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Strategic foresight-adjacent claims when the focus is the predicted nature of systems rather than methods for anticipating them. Different from Operational Tempo when the emphasis is instability and emergence rather than speed advantage.

definition: Use for predictions that influence and strategic effects will increasingly be shaped by decentralized, non-state, sub-state, or networked actors outside traditional government control.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude corporate power unless private firms/platforms are the main actors. Exclude identity communities unless the emphasis is distributed strategic agency.
inclusionCriteria: Criminal syndicates; influencers; online communities; decentralized movements; city-states; betting markets; private activist networks; distributed influence actors.
name: Non-State Actors & Distributed Influence Power
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Public–Private Integration when the focus is decentralized or non-state influence power rather than commercial integration with the state. Different from Societal Transformation when the focus is actors exercising influence rather than broad social change.

definition: Frameworks asserting that information, cognition, narratives, and perception are foundational elements of strategic competition and warfare rather than merely supporting functions.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude narrower audience-analysis, message-design, platform-dynamics, or specific deception frameworks unless the main claim is that information itself is the decisive competitive terrain.
inclusionCriteria: Use for concepts that place information, cognition, perception, or narrative at the center of competition, warfighting, deterrence, or national power.
name: Information-Centric Competition
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Information Environment & Ecosystem Models, but this tag emphasizes strategic primacy; near Cross-Domain & Integrated Competition Frameworks, but this tag is less about synchronization of instruments.

definition: Concepts focused on protecting, shaping, exploiting, or understanding human cognition, decision-making, epistemic resilience, and psychological vulnerabilities in contested information environments.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude general media literacy unless framed as cognitive defense; exclude AI or platform issues unless the central concern is human decision protection.
inclusionCriteria: Use for cognitive security, decision resilience, cognitive vulnerabilities, epistemic defense, psychological protection, and decision-quality protection.
name: Cognitive Security & Decision Protection
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Media Literacy & Cognitive Preparedness, but broader and more security-oriented; near Human Factors & Behavioral Design, but focused on contested cognition and protection.

definition: Frameworks describing how stories, symbols, myths, identity, emotion, and cultural meaning shape perception, legitimacy, mobilization, and collective behavior.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude simple messaging tactics unless they invoke meaning-making, identity, or narrative logic; exclude strategic culture unless focused on cultural/ideological competition over time.
inclusionCriteria: Use for narrative theory, identity-based influence, symbols, myths, cultural meaning, legitimacy narratives, grievance stories, and mobilizing frames.
name: Narrative, Identity & Meaning-Making
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Strategic Culture & Ideological Competition, but this tag focuses on meaning-making mechanisms; near Narrative/Messaging practice tags, but this is conceptual.

definition: Concepts examining how platforms, algorithms, amplification systems, personalization, virality, and attention dynamics shape modern influence and information environments.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude specific platform technologies unless discussed conceptually; exclude broader ecosystem models that do not foreground attention or algorithms.
inclusionCriteria: Use for theoretical discussions of attention scarcity, platform incentives, algorithmic curation, personalization, virality, and engagement-driven information exposure.
name: Attention Economies & Algorithmic Information Ecosystems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Platform, Algorithmic & Information Ecosystem Concepts; consider merging or using this when emphasis is on attention-economy theory rather than platform mechanics.

definition: Frameworks emphasizing feedback loops, adaptation, emergence, cybernetics, systems thinking, complexity, and nonlinear interactions in strategic competition.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude simple forecasting or foresight unless complexity/nonlinearity is central; exclude campaign integration unless modeled as a complex adaptive system.
inclusionCriteria: Use for complexity theory, systems thinking, feedback loops, emergence, adaptation, nonlinearity, cybernetic control, and dynamic competition models.
name: Complex Adaptive Systems & Cybernetic Competition
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Innovation, Experimentation & Foresight, but this tag concerns system dynamics; near Information Environment & Ecosystem Models, but emphasizes complexity mechanisms.

definition: Concepts describing how states and non-state actors conduct persistent influence, deception, coercion, gray-zone activity, and sub-threshold competition.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude operational campaign mechanics unless the focus is the competitive model; exclude governance/legal competition unless law and norms are central.
inclusionCriteria: Use for adversarial influence models, active measures, coercion, gray-zone competition, hybrid competition, strategic deception, and competitive influence theory.
name: Strategic Influence & Adversarial Competition Models
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Persistent Competition Concepts, but this tag emphasizes adversarial influence and coercive competition; near Deception & Reflexive Control Frameworks, but broader.

definition: Frameworks emphasizing decentralized but aligned coordination across governments, militaries, industry, academia, civil society, and alliances to compete effectively in the information environment.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude specific organizations unless the item discusses a coordination model; exclude campaign synchronization limited to military domains.
inclusionCriteria: Use for whole-of-society approaches, distributed alignment, networked coordination, interagency/cross-sector integration, and societal mobilization for information competition.
name: Distributed Coordination & Whole-of-Society Integration
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Campaign Integration & Cross-Domain Synchronization, but this tag includes civil society and whole-of-society alignment; near Cross-Domain frameworks, but more societal.

definition: Concepts focused on experimentation, evaluation, measurement, rapid feedback, lessons learned, and iterative adaptation in operational and strategic contexts.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude general organizational learning unless focused on operational assessment; exclude research rigor unless it is tied to operational adaptation.
inclusionCriteria: Use for assessment frameworks, feedback loops, experimentation, lessons learned, metrics, evaluation, adaptation cycles, and learning while campaigning.
name: Operational Learning, Assessment & Adaptation
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Organizational Learning & Talent Development, but this tag is about operations and assessment; near Innovation & Experimentation, but more evaluation-focused.

definition: Frameworks describing how environments, incentives, habits, heuristics, and behavioral conditions shape human action and decision-making.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude cognitive security unless framed in adversarial protection terms; exclude audience segmentation unless the focus is profiling or targeting.
inclusionCriteria: Use for behavior change theory, choice architecture, incentives, heuristics, habits, motivation, behavioral design, and human factors affecting action.
name: Human Factors & Behavioral Design
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Cognitive Security & Decision Protection, but less security-specific; near Targeting, Segmentation & Audience Analysis, but focused on behavioral mechanisms.

definition: Concepts related to how societies construct, validate, distribute, and defend knowledge, truth claims, trust, and shared reality.
exclusionCriteria: Exclude narrow verification technologies unless the concept is knowledge-system defense; exclude platform dynamics unless about shared reality or knowledge production.
inclusionCriteria: Use for epistemology, knowledge validation, truth infrastructure, institutional trust, expertise, provenance, shared reality, and sensemaking systems.
name: Epistemic Infrastructure & Knowledge Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Trust/verification trend tags, but this is conceptual; near Information Environment & Ecosystem Models, but centered on knowledge and truth.

definition: Concepts focused on artificial intelligence, automation, computational persuasion, machine-assisted influence, AI-enabled targeting, and algorithmic decision systems.

definition: Recommendations that improve operational continuity, combat effectiveness, command and control, communications, ISR, PACE planning, PNT resilience, UAS employment, ACE, sensor fusion, or other warfighting support adaptations under contested conditions.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for societal cognitive resilience or general technology governance. Do not use for integrated information operations unless combat-support resilience is the main action.
inclusionCriteria: Use for hardening C2, building PACE plans, improving PNT alternatives, integrating ISR, enabling UAS operations, adapting ACE, ensuring communications resilience, protecting operational infrastructure, or supporting kinetic/non-kinetic warfighting effectiveness.
name: Operational Resilience & Warfighting Enablement
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Integration when systems/functions are synchronized; choose Operational Resilience when the emphasis is warfighting continuity. Near Data/AI when analytic systems support operations; choose Operational Resilience if the key outcome is mission assurance.

definition: Actions that improve anticipatory analysis, futures thinking, threatcasting, complexity reasoning, visualization, historical analogy, scenario planning, horizon scanning, and sensemaking under uncertainty.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for campaign planning unless the emphasis is future uncertainty or complexity. Do not use for assessment unless the focus is measurement rather than anticipatory sensemaking.
inclusionCriteria: Use for threatcasting, scenario planning, futures analysis, complexity models, visualization tools, historical analogy, anticipatory intelligence, sensemaking frameworks, and efforts to understand nonlinear or emergent information-environment dynamics.
name: Strategic Foresight, Complexity & Sensemaking
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Assessment, Measurement & Research Rigor when analysis is systematic; choose Foresight when the goal is anticipation and sensemaking. Near Education when wargames are used for learning; choose Foresight if they are used to explore future conditions.

definition: Recommendations that protect truthfulness, transparency, proportionality, civil liberties, democratic values, legitimacy, accountability, and responsible restraint in information, influence, cognitive security, or technology-related activities.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for legal authorities alone unless the core issue is normative legitimacy. Do not use for platform governance unless values-based guardrails are the main point.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the item recommends ethical constraints, transparency, civil-liberties safeguards, legitimacy protection, truth-based influence, democratic accountability, responsible AI, restraint, or avoiding manipulative practices.
name: Ethics, Legitimacy & Democratic Guardrails
nearNeighborDistinctions: Near Technology Standards when guardrails are implemented through technical rules; choose Ethics when legitimacy and democratic values are central. Near Narrative when truthfulness shapes messaging; choose Ethics if the main recommendation is restraint or credibility protection.

definition: Military commands, units, task forces, headquarters, service components, or operational formations responsible for planning, commanding, integrating, employing, or executing warfighting and information-related activities.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for civilian agencies, contractors, think tanks, media organizations, or broad identity communities unless the item specifically refers to a military unit or command role.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the actor is a military command, operational unit, service component, headquarters, task force, or force element with direct operational planning or execution responsibilities.
name: Military Commands, Forces, & Operational Units
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Defense & National Security Agencies, which covers government agencies and security institutions rather than operational military formations. Different from Integrated coordination mechanisms, which refers to linking bodies across sectors rather than the units themselves.

definition: Government defense, intelligence, homeland security, cyber, law-enforcement-adjacent, or national security agencies responsible for security policy, intelligence, operations, resilience, threat reduction, or protective missions.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for military combat units, civilian legislatures/courts/regulators, private technology firms, or academic institutions unless the item emphasizes a national-security agency function.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the actor is a named or implied government security agency, intelligence organization, homeland security body, cyber agency, or national security institution.
name: Defense & National Security Agencies
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Military Commands, Forces, & Operational Units, which covers force-employment organizations. Different from Civilian Governance, Policy, & Oversight Institutions, which covers policy, law, budget, and oversight bodies rather than operational security agencies.

definition: Civilian government bodies, legislatures, courts, regulators, diplomatic offices, oversight institutions, or policy offices that shape legal authorities, legitimacy, budgets, interagency coordination, public accountability, or foreign policy direction.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for operational military commands, intelligence agencies, private-sector platforms, or standards bodies unless the emphasis is civilian governance, public authority, or oversight.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the item concerns lawmakers, courts, regulators, civilian departments, diplomatic institutions, oversight committees, or policy offices shaping authorities, constraints, budgets, or governance choices.
name: Civilian Governance, Policy, & Oversight Institutions
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Standards, Governance Regimes, & Regulatory Ecosystems, which focuses on rule systems and regimes themselves. Different from Defense & National Security Agencies, which focuses on security agencies carrying out missions.

definition: State competitors, proxy forces, terrorist groups, regime-aligned activists, state media organs, covert operators, or hostile influence entities engaged in coercion, disinformation, gray-zone activity, lawfare, cyber-enabled influence, or strategic competition.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for neutral foreign partners, domestic civil society, ordinary target audiences, or platforms unless they are explicitly acting as hostile influence agents or instruments.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the actor is described as a hostile, adversarial, competitor, proxy, regime-aligned, or malign influence participant.
name: Adversary States, Proxies, & Hostile Influence Actors
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Media, Journalism, Broadcasting, & Information Distribution when the media actor is specifically state-controlled or hostile. Different from Identity, Cultural, Religious, & Demographic Communities unless the community is acting as a proxy or hostile movement.

definition: Multinational alliances, partner networks, treaty organizations, international courts, regional blocs, coalition task structures, or international institutions that enable collective action, interoperability, norms, legal pressure, or multinational coordination.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for single-nation agencies, informal cross-sector partnerships, or standards regimes unless the item emphasizes multinational collective action or international institutional authority.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the item refers to NATO-like alliances, coalitions, international organizations, regional blocs, multinational legal bodies, or partner networks as actors or enabling structures.
name: Alliances, Coalitions, & International Organizations
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Cross-Sector Coordination & Public–Private Integration Mechanisms, which links sectors rather than nations. Different from Standards, Governance Regimes, & Regulatory Ecosystems, which concerns rules and frameworks rather than the organizations themselves.

definition: Social media platforms, AI companies, cloud providers, internet governance entities, digital ecosystems, telecom-like platform operators, or technical infrastructure organizations that shape communication, data flows, algorithmic exposure, identity, access, or platform power.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for defense contractors unless the item emphasizes platform or digital-infrastructure power. Do not use for technologies themselves unless the organization operating or governing them is central.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the actor is a technology platform, AI firm, cloud provider, digital infrastructure company, social media ecosystem, or internet governance organization.
name: Technology Platforms, AI Firms, & Digital Infrastructure
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Defense Industry, Contractors, & Commercial Partners when the firm is primarily a defense vendor. Different from Media, Journalism, Broadcasting, & Information Distribution when the actor is a platform rather than a content producer or broadcaster.

definition: Private firms, defense contractors, vendors, consultants, investment groups, commercial partners, or industry teams supporting national security missions, technology transition, analytics, training, experimentation, or operational capability development.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for general technology platforms unless the item emphasizes their national security partnership or contractor role. Do not use for academic/research organizations unless they are acting as commercial partners.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the actor is a contractor, vendor, defense company, consultant, commercial partner, accelerator, investor, or industry participant supporting government or military needs.
name: Defense Industry, Contractors, & Commercial Partners
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Technology Platforms, AI Firms, & Digital Infrastructure, which covers platform power and digital ecosystems. Different from Cross-Sector Coordination mechanisms, which are the partnership structures rather than individual firms.

definition: Universities, research centers, think tanks, national labs, journals, archives, and knowledge-producing institutions that develop theory, evidence, technical expertise, doctrine, foresight, analytic methods, or conceptual frameworks.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for training schools unless the emphasis is workforce instruction. Do not use for contractors unless the emphasis is commercial delivery rather than knowledge production.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the item concerns knowledge production, scholarship, research translation, analytic frameworks, theoretical development, or expert evidence from academic/research institutions.
name: Research, Academia, Think Tanks, & Knowledge Institutions
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Education, Training, PME, & Workforce Pipelines, which focuses on developing people and professional skills. Different from Professional Associations, Practitioner Networks, & Communities of Interest, which convene communities rather than primarily producing research.

definition: Schools, military education systems, training centers, professional military education programs, certification programs, courses, or workforce-development institutions that build expertise, doctrine familiarity, technical literacy, analytic skill, or professional identity.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for research institutions unless the item emphasizes training. Do not use for practitioner networks unless they are functioning as formal education or workforce-development channels.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the organization or community is primarily responsible for teaching, training, credentialing, professional formation, or workforce pipeline development.
name: Education, Training, PME, & Workforce Pipelines
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Research, Academia, Think Tanks, & Knowledge Institutions, which emphasizes knowledge production. Different from Professional Associations, Practitioner Networks, & Communities of Interest, which emphasizes convening and diffusion among practitioners.

definition: News outlets, broadcasters, state or public media, journalism ecosystems, publishers, creators, and information-distribution institutions that shape public awareness, narratives, trust, agenda setting, and issue salience.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for social platforms unless the platform itself is the central actor. Do not use for adversary state media when the hostile influence function is primary unless dual coding is needed.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the actor is a media organization, broadcaster, journalist network, news ecosystem, publisher, content distributor, or information outlet shaping public narratives or awareness.
name: Media, Journalism, Broadcasting, & Information Distribution
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Technology Platforms, AI Firms, & Digital Infrastructure, which covers platform infrastructure and algorithms. Different from Adversary States, Proxies, & Hostile Influence Actors when media are explicitly used as hostile state instruments.

definition: NGOs, nonprofit groups, foundations, advocacy organizations, civic groups, community organizations, and resilience-oriented institutions working on democracy support, media literacy, counter-disinformation, public trust, human rights, or community protection.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for government agencies, private firms, media organizations, or broad identity groups unless the item refers to an organized civic or nonprofit actor.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the actor is a nongovernmental or civic organization oriented toward public resilience, rights protection, civic education, democratic defense, community protection, or counter-disinformation.
name: Civil Society, NGOs, & Public Resilience Organizations
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Identity, Cultural, Religious, & Demographic Communities, which covers audiences and social groups. Different from Cross-Sector Coordination mechanisms, which refers to the integration mechanism connecting civil society with other sectors.

definition: Associations, conferences, working groups, professional networks, communities of practice, and practitioner forums that convene experts, diffuse lessons, build shared language, and connect researchers, operators, policymakers, and technologists.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for formal education institutions, research centers, or cross-sector mechanisms unless the item emphasizes professional convening and community-building.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the actor is a professional association, working group, conference, practitioner network, or community of interest that creates exchange, shared identity, standards of practice, or lesson diffusion.
name: Professional Associations, Practitioner Networks, & Communities of Interest
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Education, Training, PME, & Workforce Pipelines, which focuses on formal instruction. Different from Cross-Sector Coordination & Public–Private Integration Mechanisms, which emphasizes operational integration across sectors.

definition: Populations or communities organized around identity, grievance, ideology, religion, geography, culture, language, generation, diaspora status, or social position that function as audiences, targets, participants, interpreters, or meaning-making communities.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for formal organizations, NGOs, media outlets, or military units unless the item centers on their identity-community role as an audience or meaning-making group.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the item refers to an audience or community defined by identity, culture, religion, demography, geography, ideology, grievance, or shared social meaning.
name: Identity, Cultural, Religious, & Demographic Communities
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Civil Society, NGOs, & Public Resilience Organizations, which covers formal civic organizations. Different from Adversary States, Proxies, & Hostile Influence Actors unless the community is mobilized as a hostile proxy or movement.

definition: Formal or informal mechanisms, partnerships, fusion cells, consortia, liaison structures, information-sharing channels, or coordination bodies that connect government, industry, academia, civil society, and operational communities for innovation, crisis response, resilience, research translation, or operational information sharing.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for individual organizations unless the item emphasizes their role in a multi-sector integration mechanism. Do not use for alliances unless the cross-sector rather than multinational character is central.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the item focuses on the mechanism or structure that integrates multiple sectors, rather than one participating organization alone.
name: Cross-Sector Coordination & Public–Private Integration Mechanisms
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Alliances, Coalitions, & International Organizations, which emphasizes multinational collective action. Different from Defense Industry or Civil Society categories, which identify individual sectors rather than integration structures.

definition: Standards bodies, governance frameworks, compliance regimes, legal structures, institutional rule sets, accreditation systems, platform oversight regimes, or regulatory ecosystems that define acceptable behavior, legitimacy, accountability, interoperability, or operational constraints.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for individual regulators, legislatures, or courts unless the emphasis is the broader governance regime. Do not use for alliances unless the focus is their standards or rule systems.
inclusionCriteria: Use when the item concerns the regime, rule set, standard-setting process, compliance ecosystem, regulatory architecture, or governance framework that structures organizational behavior.
name: Standards, Governance Regimes, & Regulatory Ecosystems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Different from Civilian Governance, Policy, & Oversight Institutions, which identifies specific policy/oversight bodies. Different from Governance, Moderation, & Information Control Systems in the technology category, which refers to technical systems rather than organizational/regulatory ecosystems.

definition: Systems used to observe, monitor, collect, detect, map, ingest, or track behaviors, narratives, signals, populations, communications, infrastructure, or operational conditions across the information environment.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for systems primarily used to interpret or simulate collected data; code those as Assessment, Modeling, & Decision-Support Systems. Do not use for delivery channels unless the emphasis is collection rather than dissemination.
inclusionCriteria: Use for tools that collect, ingest, detect, monitor, map, or track signals, narratives, audiences, infrastructure, communications, or behavioral indicators in the information environment.
name: Information Environment Sensing & Collection Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Assessment, Modeling, & Decision-Support Systems by function: sensing/collection gathers observations; assessment/modeling analyzes or forecasts them. Distinguish from Identity, Persona, & Social Graph Systems when the focus is broad IE monitoring rather than identity linkage.

definition: Technologies and frameworks used to analyze, model, forecast, simulate, visualize, classify, quantify, or assess cognitive, behavioral, informational, or operational dynamics.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for raw sensing pipelines unless the item emphasizes analysis or modeling. Do not use for training environments unless the primary purpose is operator preparation rather than analytic assessment.
inclusionCriteria: Use for analytic, modeling, simulation, visualization, classification, forecasting, decision-support, or assessment tools that help users understand IE, cognitive, behavioral, or operational dynamics.
name: Assessment, Modeling, & Decision-Support Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Information Environment Sensing & Collection Systems by output: this cluster transforms observations into assessments, forecasts, models, dashboards, or decisions. Distinguish from Training, Simulation, & Operational Preparation Systems when simulation supports analysis rather than rehearsal.

definition: Platforms, ecosystems, media channels, communications infrastructures, and dissemination mechanisms used to distribute, amplify, synchronize, coordinate, or deliver narratives and influence content.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use when the item focuses on platform algorithms or recommendation mechanics; code those as Algorithmic Amplification & Platform Dynamics. Do not use for governance or moderation mechanisms controlling visibility.
inclusionCriteria: Use for channels, media ecosystems, broadcast systems, social platforms, collaboration tools, or dissemination mechanisms used to distribute, amplify, coordinate, or deliver narratives and influence content.
name: Influence Delivery & Communication Platforms
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Algorithmic Amplification & Platform Dynamics by emphasis: delivery platforms are the channels; algorithmic dynamics are the visibility and engagement mechanics operating within them. Distinguish from Infrastructure, Connectivity, & Information Backbone Systems when the focus is communicative reach rather than technical backbone.

definition: Algorithmic, engagement-driven, or platform-native mechanisms that shape visibility, virality, emotional contagion, recommendation pathways, audience exposure, or online coordination dynamics.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use merely because an item mentions a social platform; use Influence Delivery & Communication Platforms if the focus is the channel itself. Do not use for formal moderation or control systems unless algorithmic ranking is central.
inclusionCriteria: Use for algorithmic, engagement-driven, recommender, ranking, virality, bot-amplification, emotional-contagion, echo-chamber, or platform-native coordination dynamics that shape what audiences see and share.
name: Algorithmic Amplification & Platform Dynamics
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Influence Delivery & Communication Platforms by mechanism: this cluster concerns algorithmic selection, amplification, and engagement dynamics, not simply the existence of a communications channel. Distinguish from Governance, Moderation, & Information Control Systems when the issue is visibility optimization rather than rule enforcement or suppression.

definition: Systems that regulate, authenticate, moderate, filter, verify, suppress, govern, label, or control information visibility, platform participation, or digital ecosystem boundaries.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for general platform dynamics unless moderation, labeling, censorship, verification, or governance is the core function. Do not use for protective resilience tools unless the emphasis is maintaining access under repression.
inclusionCriteria: Use for systems that regulate, authenticate, filter, moderate, label, suppress, verify, govern, or control information visibility, participation, or ecosystem boundaries.
name: Governance, Moderation, & Information Control Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Algorithmic Amplification & Platform Dynamics by intent: governance/control systems set rules, labels, gates, or restrictions; algorithmic dynamics optimize exposure and engagement. Distinguish from Resilience, Circumvention, & Protective Systems when the item concerns circumventing controls rather than imposing them.

definition: AI/ML, generative systems, NLP, automation, autonomous agents, and computational pipelines that accelerate, personalize, optimize, generate, or scale informational and operational activities.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for all software-enabled tools by default; reserve for cases where AI, ML, automation, computational influence, or autonomous processing is central. Synthetic media should be coded separately when media fabrication itself is the main issue.
inclusionCriteria: Use for AI/ML, NLP, generative AI, autonomous agents, automation pipelines, or computational systems that generate, accelerate, personalize, optimize, assess, or scale informational and operational activity.
name: AI, Automation, & Computational Influence Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Synthetic Media & Reality Manipulation Systems when the output is fabricated media or altered reality representations. Distinguish from Assessment, Modeling, & Decision-Support Systems when AI is not the salient feature of the analytic system.

definition: Cyber, EW, spectrum, networking, and technical-access capabilities used to exploit, defend, deny, manipulate, degrade, or secure digital and electromagnetic systems.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for general IT infrastructure unless exploitation, access, defense, denial, or electromagnetic effects are central. Do not use for integrated multi-domain campaigns unless the emphasis is synchronized operational architecture.
inclusionCriteria: Use for cyber, EW, spectrum, network access, technical exploitation, defensive cyber, spoofing, PNT, or electromagnetic capabilities used to exploit, defend, deny, degrade, manipulate, or secure digital and electromagnetic systems.
name: Cyber, Electromagnetic, & Technical Access Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Infrastructure, Connectivity, & Information Backbone Systems by purpose: cyber/EW systems act on technical access, denial, manipulation, or defense; backbone systems provide communications and connectivity. Distinguish from Integrated Information Warfare & Multi-Domain Operational Systems when cyber/EW is one part of a larger synchronized campaign.

definition: Foundational infrastructures that enable persistent communications, storage, networking, broadcasting, cloud access, synchronization, transmission, or resilience across the information ecosystem.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for cyber exploitation or EW effects on infrastructure unless the technical action is central. Do not use for influence platforms unless the emphasis is user-facing dissemination rather than backbone connectivity.
inclusionCriteria: Use for foundational communications, networking, broadcast, cloud, satellite, storage, enterprise IT, telecom, and transmission infrastructures that enable persistent information flow or resilience.
name: Infrastructure, Connectivity, & Information Backbone Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Influence Delivery & Communication Platforms by layer: backbone systems enable information flow; delivery platforms are user-facing channels for communication and influence. Distinguish from Cyber, Electromagnetic, & Technical Access Systems when the item concerns infrastructure operation rather than exploitation or denial.

definition: Systems that identify, authenticate, infer, construct, track, manipulate, or operationalize identity, social relationships, personas, or reputational associations.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for broad audience monitoring unless identity linkage, persona construction, or relationship mapping is central. Do not use for biometric human-state sensing unless the focus is physiology/cognition rather than identity.
inclusionCriteria: Use for systems that identify, authenticate, infer, construct, track, resolve, manipulate, or operationalize identities, personas, relationships, reputations, or social graphs.
name: Identity, Persona, & Social Graph Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Information Environment Sensing & Collection Systems when the analytic unit is identity, persona, or relational graph rather than broad IE collection. Distinguish from Human-State, Neurocognitive, & Biometric Systems when biometrics are used to infer state rather than identify a person.

definition: Technologies that measure, infer, augment, interface with, manipulate, or model cognition, emotion, physiology, neural activity, or psychological states.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for identity-only biometric recognition unless human state or cognition is central. Do not use for synthetic media or XR reality manipulation unless physiological/cognitive measurement or augmentation is the main focus.
inclusionCriteria: Use for technologies that measure, infer, augment, interface with, manipulate, or model cognition, emotion, physiology, neural activity, attention, psychological state, or human performance.
name: Human-State, Neurocognitive, & Biometric Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Identity, Persona, & Social Graph Systems by purpose: this cluster concerns human state, cognition, physiology, or augmentation; identity systems resolve who someone is. Distinguish from Synthetic Media & Reality Manipulation Systems when manipulation is representational rather than neurocognitive or physiological.

definition: Systems that fabricate, alter, simulate, or manipulate media, sensory experience, or representations of reality.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for general AI systems unless the salient output is synthetic or manipulated media/reality. Do not use for influence delivery channels unless the focus is distribution rather than fabrication.
inclusionCriteria: Use for systems that fabricate, alter, simulate, remix, or manipulate media, sensory experience, representations, or perceived reality.
name: Synthetic Media & Reality Manipulation Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from AI, Automation, & Computational Influence Systems when generative AI is used specifically to fabricate or alter media. Distinguish from Influence Delivery & Communication Platforms when the issue is what is created rather than where it is disseminated.

definition: Simulations, synthetic environments, wargames, exercises, rehearsal environments, and educational/training systems designed to prepare operators or test concepts.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for modeling tools whose main purpose is analytic assessment rather than training or preparation. Do not use for integrated operational systems unless the system is primarily for rehearsal or preparation.
inclusionCriteria: Use for wargames, exercises, simulations, synthetic environments, rehearsal tools, educational platforms, and operational-preparation systems designed to train operators or test concepts.
name: Training, Simulation, & Operational Preparation Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Assessment, Modeling, & Decision-Support Systems by end use: training systems prepare people and organizations; assessment systems inform analysis and decisions. Distinguish from Integrated Information Warfare & Multi-Domain Operational Systems when the item concerns operational execution rather than rehearsal.

definition: Architectures and operational ecosystems that synchronize cyber, ISR, EW, IO, C2, AI, space, and influence capabilities into integrated effects campaigns.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for a single technology domain unless integration across domains/functions is the core emphasis. Do not use for generic decision-support tools unless they are part of synchronized operational effects architecture.
inclusionCriteria: Use for architectures, operational ecosystems, or system-of-systems approaches that synchronize cyber, ISR, EW, IO, C2, AI, space, influence, or kinetic/non-kinetic capabilities into integrated effects campaigns.
name: Integrated Information Warfare & Multi-Domain Operational Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Cyber, Electromagnetic, & Technical Access Systems when cyber/EW is embedded in broader multi-domain orchestration. Distinguish from Assessment, Modeling, & Decision-Support Systems when the system is for operational synchronization and execution rather than analysis alone.

definition: Technologies and methods designed to preserve access, continuity, survivability, trust, privacy, or operational effectiveness under contested or adversarial conditions.
exclusionCriteria: Do not use for governance or control systems that impose restrictions; use this cluster for countermeasures, protection, continuity, or circumvention. Do not use for general infrastructure unless resilience or survivability is central.
inclusionCriteria: Use for technologies, tools, or methods designed to preserve access, continuity, survivability, trust, privacy, authenticity, or operational effectiveness under contested, censored, degraded, or adversarial conditions.
name: Resilience, Circumvention, & Protective Systems
nearNeighborDistinctions: Distinguish from Governance, Moderation, & Information Control Systems by direction of action: this cluster resists disruption or control; governance/control systems regulate or restrict. Distinguish from Infrastructure, Connectivity, & Information Backbone Systems when resilience/circumvention is the defining purpose rather than ordinary connectivity.
